title: Letter combinations and nasal vowels
goal: By the end of this lesson you can read common letter combinations like ou, oi, eau, ch and gn correctly, pronounce the three main nasal vowels, and recognise the Quebec 'paère / faète' vowels.

learn.h: Vowel combinations: two letters, one sound
body: French often writes one sound with two or three letters. Once you know the combinations, you can read almost any word aloud.
The big ones: *ou* sounds like 'oo' (*vous*), *oi* sounds like 'wa' (*moi*), *au* and *eau* both sound like 'oh' (*auto*, *beau*), and *ai* / *ei* sound like the 'e' in 'bed' (*lait*, *neige*).
learn.tip: u alone = [ü]; ou = 'oo'. Tu (you) vs tout (all).

body: *ch* sounds like English 'sh' (*chat*, *chocolat*), never like 'ch' in 'church'. *gn* sounds like 'ny' in 'canyon' (*montagne*, *champignon*). *qu* is simply 'k' (*qui*, *quatre*). *ph* is 'f' (*photo*) and *th* is just 't' (*thé*).
*ill* after a vowel or in most words sounds like 'y': *fille* (fee-y), *famille*, *travail*. Three common exceptions keep a real l sound: *ville*, *mille*, *tranquille*.
A nasal vowel is a vowel said partly through the nose. In writing, it is a vowel followed by *n* or *m*. The n or m itself is NOT pronounced: it only tells you the vowel is nasal.
French has three nasal vowels you must master (a fourth, *un*, has merged with *in* for many speakers in France, but Quebecers keep it distinct).
learn.tip: Never say the n: bon is 'bõ', not 'bonn'.

learn.h: When n and m are NOT nasal
body: If the *n* or *m* is followed by a vowel, or doubled (*nn*, *mm*), the vowel is NOT nasal and the consonant is pronounced: *bon* (nasal) but *bonne* (bonn), *an* (nasal) but *année* (a-né), *un* (nasal) but *une* (ün).
This is why many feminine forms 'open up' the nasal: *américain* / *américaine*, *italien* / *italienne*.

In casual Quebec speech, a long vowel in the last syllable of a word often slides into two sounds (a diphthong). *Père* sounds like 'paère', *fête* like 'faète', *mère* like 'maère', *tête* like 'taète'.

This happens mainly with long vowels: è/ê before r, v, z, j, or written ê; the long vowels in *neige*, *chaise*, *rose*, *fleur*, *pâte*. It is a feature of informal speech, stronger in some regions and speakers than others. In careful speech (news, school) you will hear less of it.

examples.note: ou = oo; on is nasal in bon
ai = eh, au = oh, ch = sh
fille has a y sound; ville has a real l

examples.fr: Le café au lait, c'est bon.
Il y a de la neige.
examples.note: ei = eh; in Quebec, neige can slide: 'naèje'

examples.fr: Mon père est à la maison.

examples.note: bonne is NOT nasal; in Quebec, fête can sound like 'faète'
année is not nasal (n + vowel); an is nasal

quebec.intro: In everyday Quebec speech, long vowels at the end of a word often 'slide' into a diphthong: père sounds like paère, fête like faète. It is informal; careful speech uses the plain vowel.

items.note: in Quebec, bonne fête is the usual birthday wish
a light diphthong; you will hear it all winter

drills.q: Which word has a NASAL vowel?
drills.why: In bon, the n ends the word, so the vowel is nasal. In the others, n is followed by a vowel or doubled.

drills.q: In which word does 'ill' keep a real L sound?
drills.why: ville, mille and tranquille are the common exceptions.
eau and au both sound like 'oh'.

drills.q: In casual Quebec speech, 'père' often sounds like…
drills.why: Long vowels slide into a diphthong: paère.

drills.a: Mon père est à la maison.

drills.why: Bonne fête is what you'll hear most in Quebec.
Il fait chaud for the weather; c'est chaud for a thing.

vocab.ex: Il y a de la neige.
Ma mère est à la maison.

pron.tip: ou = oo; u = ee with rounded lips. Keep them apart.
eau, au = oh. The final letters are silent.
Three nasals: ahn, an, ohn. Never pronounce the n.
Standard: pèr, fèt. Casual Quebec: paère, faète.

dialogue.fr: Merci, ma belle! Tu es à Montréal?
dialogue.en: Thanks, sweetie! Are you in Montreal?
Yes. It's snowing a lot here.

dialogue.fr: Ici, il fait chaud! Ton père est au café.
dialogue.en: Here it's hot! Your father is at the café.

dialogue.fr: Le chat est à la maison, avec moi.
dialogue.en: The cat is at home, with me.

dialogue.fr: Bonne journée, maman. Bonne fête encore!
dialogue.en: Have a good day, Mom. Happy birthday again!

questions.q: What is the weather like in Montreal?

speak.prompt: Read aloud, paying attention to the nasal vowels: 'Un bon vin blanc.'
speak.model: uhn bõ van blahn: no n is pronounced.

speak.prompt: Read aloud: 'Le chat noir boit de l'eau.'
speak.model: luh sha nwar bwa duh lo

speak.prompt: Wish someone happy birthday the standard way, then imitate the casual Quebec vowel.

write.prompt: Write 4–5 short sentences using at least five of this lesson's words. Circle every nasal vowel.
write.model: Mon père est à la maison. Le pain est bon. Il neige en ville. Ma fille boit de l'eau. Bonne fête, maman!

quiz.q: In a nasal vowel, the n or m is…
quiz.why: It only signals that the vowel is nasal.
In une, the n is followed by e, so it is pronounced: ün.
qu = k in nearly all French words.

quiz.q: Which pair shows the Quebec diphthong?
quiz.why: The long ê slides into 'aè' in casual speech.
French has no English th sound: thé = té.

quiz.q: Which spelling does NOT give the [ahn] sound?
